comparator.name: Linguistics
comparator.sourceNotes: The formal 2026-2027 regulations define the redesigned curriculum for the student cohort entering in 2026. They account for the complete 180 EC as 60 EC in Year 1, 60 EC in Year 2, a 30-EC minor and three 10-EC graduation-portfolio seminars in Year 3. The first-listed current Faculty-Wide Course option, Cultural Heritage: Heritage in a Changing World, is used as the neutral official-order tie-break. Students choose three of five graduation seminars; Neurolinguistics, Psycholinguistics and Developmental Language Disorders, and Syntax are the first three in the formal order and are selected independently of UCR fit. These restricted choices are not named formal routes, so no route is assigned. The current public programme page was rechecked on 14 October 2026 and continues to describe the programme's language-and-brain, language-disorder and theoretical-linguistics structure; the cohort-specific OER remains controlling where the public page presents a different later curriculum display.

trace: develops cleaning, visualisation and analysis of datasets including text data, supplying an introductory empirical language-data workflow rather than linguistic analysis
studies neural networks, text classification, large language models and generative AI; it supports language-technology questions without teaching formal or computational linguistics
supplies the linear-algebra and calculus foundation formally required before Neural Networks & Deep Learning
examines agency, personal identity, time and the self as conceptual questions about minded persons; it is philosophy of cognition rather than linguistics
provides neural anatomy, cellular neuroscience and laboratory observation as a biological foundation for asking how language is implemented in the brain
studies sensory processing, perception, action and motor control, giving concrete cognitive mechanisms relevant to spoken-language perception and production without specialising in speech
examines memory, attention, executive function and cognitive control that constrain language comprehension and production
directly studies psycholinguistic language comprehension, production, acquisition, impairment and the neuroscience of language
introduces psychology, brain systems and the effects of brain injury, providing the required foundation for later cognition and psycholinguistics courses
studies social cognition, attitudes, groups and social influence as the interpersonal context in which language and persuasion operate
develops experimental design and multivariate statistical methods for behavioural and psycholinguistic evidence
examines health behaviour, psychological intervention and communication in medical settings, offering context for language-related health questions without clinical-linguistics training
teaches systematic review, meta-analysis, effect sizes and evidence synthesis for evaluating behavioural and cognitive research
studies cognitive and social development across the lifespan, providing developmental context for language acquisition without a dedicated acquisition sequence
establishes rhetorical analysis and the design of persuasive messages through audience, argument, ethos, pathos and logos
provides structured second-language learning and practical Dutch use as an applied language-learning experience, not a scientific course in acquisition
directly analyses how linguistic choices in nonfiction texts create meaning, position readers and express ideology, while not teaching formal semantics
applies rhetorical theory through persuasive speaking and work with public voices and audiences
examines persuasion, framing, nudging and cognitive shortcuts as mechanisms linking language choices to audience response
develops communication through spoken, sonic, poetic and digitally mediated forms, foregrounding expressive language practice rather than linguistic structure
introduces close interpretation of literary and non-fiction texts, narrative and genre as forms of language-mediated meaning
analyses how narrative, diction, sound and other formal resources change when text is adapted to film
studies narrative, representation, sound and media technologies as systems that produce cultural meaning

alternatives.label: Language processing, cognition & communication
alternatives.concept: Combine psycholinguistics, neuroscience, cognition, development, experimental methods, text-data and language-technology methods with rhetoric, style, textual meaning and multimodal communication. This is a related-fields response to language-and-brain, language-use and scientific-language-analysis interests, not a full Linguistics, Neurolinguistics or Clinical Linguistics curriculum.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is concentrated in psycholinguistics, cognition, neuroscience, communication, text analysis and language-related data methods. The label deliberately does not claim structural, theoretical, clinical or neuroimaging-based linguistics formation.
progression: The schedule contains 24 unique courses, four per fixed semester, Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and ten level-300 courses. Every formal prerequisite occurs earlier and every course is available in its assigned term. Introduction to Brain & Behavior precedes Higher Order Functions, Perception & Action, Medical & Health Psychology, Lifespan Developmental Psychology, Psycholinguistics and Advanced Research Seminar; Mathematical Methods precedes Neural Networks & Deep Learning.

candidates.label: Clinical linguistics, neurolinguistics and speech-language disorders

selection.assessment: One complete related-fields programme passes the evidence, relevance and mechanical gates. It responds to language processing, language and the brain, language learning and use, communication, human-centred language technology and empirical analysis through actual psycholinguistics, cognition, neuroscience, development, statistics, text-data and communication content. It is explicitly not presented as Linguistics. A structural/theoretical direction cannot supply the cumulative phonology, syntax, morphology, formal semantics, pragmatics or language-change sequence. A clinical/neurolinguistics direction cannot supply speech-language pathology, dyslexia, clinical assessment, language neuroimaging or supervised clinical formation. No padded second programme is produced.

blocks: Both examine relations between mental functions and brain systems; UCR is a broad psychology and neuroscience foundation and does not teach language neuroimaging.

Both directly study language processing and psycholinguistic research; UCR covers comprehension, production, acquisition, impairment and neuroscience but does not reproduce the target's project sequence.
Both address development across childhood and later life; UCR provides broad cognitive and social developmental psychology rather than a scientific language-acquisition course.
Both examine how messages work in context and for audiences; UCR teaches rhetorical communication rather than formal linguistic pragmatics.
Both study meaning in language; UCR analyses stylistic and ideological effects of linguistic choices in texts rather than formal semantics.

Both address AI in relation to language and society; UCR teaches neural networks, text classification, large language models and generative AI, while the target component has a broader human-centred digital-society remit.
Both develop statistical methods for empirical research; UCR covers experimental design and multivariate behavioural statistics.
Structural, clinical and specialist linguistics gaps
UCR has no course in language and speech disorders or speech-language pathology.
UCR has no foundation course in phonology and syntax.
UCR has no course in language change and language contact.
UCR has no dedicated dyslexia course.
UCR has no Clinical Linguistics course or clinical language-assessment formation.
UCR has no course in linguistic morphology.
UCR has no advanced formal-semantics sequence.
UCR has no advanced syntax sequence.
The selected Faculty-Wide Course remains visible; no UCR course is presented as its equivalent.
UCR has no advanced phonology sequence.
The genuine 30-EC minor remains open and is not populated with invented UCR equivalents.
UCR has no advanced Neurolinguistics graduation seminar.
One UCR Psycholinguistics course does not reproduce the advanced graduation seminar in psycholinguistics and developmental language disorders.
UCR has no Syntax graduation seminar.

notes.text: The UCR programme combines psycholinguistics, cognitive neuroscience, development, behavioural research, text-data and language-technology methods with rhetoric, stylistics and multimodal communication. It does not reproduce the target's cumulative phonology, syntax, morphology, formal semantics, pragmatics and language-change sequence; language and speech pathology, dyslexia, clinical linguistics and neuroimaging; or specialist Linguistics graduation seminars.
